kurz: How chart type, timeframe and axis type determine which price movements look large in a chart, even before any pattern is interpreted.

bloecke.md:
A chart is a record of executed trades and not a picture of the company. It contains exactly two raw quantities, the price of the trades and the volume traded. All other elements, such as trend lines, moving averages and oscillators, are derived from these two series. A chart therefore shows what market participants have done, but not what an investment is worth. This limit applies to every interpretation.

The first decision is made with the choice of display, even before you look at the chart. Every display condenses the data, and each chart type leaves out different information in the process. When reading a chart, you therefore need to know which information is missing.

bloecke.md:
## Structure of candles and bars

A candle shows four numbers per interval. Its body extends from the opening price to the closing price, and the wicks above and below extend to the high and the low of the interval. If the closing price is above the open, the body is light, otherwise dark. A bar chart shows the same four numbers differently. A vertical line runs from the low to the high, a short horizontal tick to the left marks the open and one to the right the close.

Candlestick charts therefore contain no information that the bar chart does not also show, even though the opposite is often claimed. The difference lies in perception, as coloured areas can be scanned faster than lines. That makes reading easier but brings no advantage in forecasting.

bloecke.titel: Fourteen intervals as a candlestick and line chart
bloecke.unter: Schematic series. The candles show open, high, low and close. The overlaid line connects only the closing prices and thus corresponds to the line chart of the same data.

bloecke.md:
## Limits of the line chart

In interval 5, the line shows an unremarkable rise from 98.20 to 98.90. During the day, however, the price fell as low as 95.60, that is, 2.6% below the previous day's closing price. A stop at 96 would have been triggered without the line chart showing any trace of it. For decisions that depend on the high or low, such as stops, breakouts and volatility measures, it is therefore the wrong display.

A second example lies between intervals 7 and 8. The high of interval 7 is 101.90, the low of interval 8 is 103.00. No trading took place in this range; it is a [[price gap]]. The line chart draws a steep but continuous line there. Whether the price passed through the range or jumped over it cannot be seen from it.

Before any interpretation, clarify which information the display has removed and whether it would have changed the decision. Otherwise it remains unclear whether an impression comes from the data or from the display.

## Choice of timeframe

Each candle summarises the trading of a fixed period of time. Continuous trading on Xetra runs from 9:00 to 17:30, which is 510 minutes a day, with around 250 trading days a year. This determines how many observations a timeframe provides and thus how often it gives cause for a decision.

bloecke.titel: Observations per timeframe (calculated from 510 trading minutes and around 250 trading days)

bloecke.md:
Shorter timeframes provide no additional information about the future. They show more fluctuations around the same price. What certainly increases, on the other hand, is the number of opportunities to trade, and every trade incurs costs. With 250 round turns a year and costs of 0.10% per round turn for fees, spread and slippage, these trading costs alone add up to 25 percentage points a year. Because the costs of each round turn are deducted from the capital remaining at that point, capital at the end of the year is around 22% lower than without these costs. With 1,000 round turns, the costs add up to 100 percentage points, and capital is then around 63% lower. The timeframe therefore fixes the cost structure before the first trading rule has been formulated.

Conversely, for a question that will be decided over years, a one-minute chart is no more precise. It merely shows more short-term fluctuations.

## Volume

Below the price area, a chart usually shows one bar per interval for the quantity traded or the turnover. Apart from the price, volume is the only quantity that is measured directly and not calculated. The price shows the direction of a movement; volume shows how strongly the market is taking part in it.

In Germany, two limitations are particularly important here. First, the trading volume of a security is spread across Xetra, the regional exchanges, off-exchange direct trading and foreign trading venues. The volume bar in a broker's chart therefore shows only a section and not a picture of the entire market. Second, volume depends on the time of day. Via the Xetra Retail Service, trading takes place from 8:00 to 8:55 and from 17:30 to 22:00, and on the Frankfurt Stock Exchange from 8:00 to 22:00. In these off-peak hours, spreads are wider and volumes lower.

Opening and closing prices stand out in the chart for another reason. On Xetra, both are set in auctions according to the [[maximum executable volume principle]], that is, at the price at which the highest volume can be executed. Unlike arbitrary prices from continuous trading, they pool the orders of many market participants and are therefore the most broadly agreed prices of the day.

A price breakout with a conspicuous volume bar at 20:30 means little. In off-peak hours with low trading, a single larger order is enough to produce the high, low and volume of an entire interval. Before interpreting a volume signal, you should therefore check the trading venue, the time and the share of the security's total volume.

## Linear and logarithmic axis

On a linear axis, an equal vertical distance stands for an equal amount. On a [[Logarithmic scale|logarithmic]] axis, it stands for an equal percentage. For wealth, what counts is the percentage change. A fall from 100 to 90 costs the same proportion as one from 1,000 to 900, but on the linear axis the second fall is drawn ten times as large.

Over short periods, this difference hardly matters. Over long periods, it changes the shape of the curve and thus what the chart says. The following illustrative calculation shows two series that start at €100 and both end at €2,172 after forty years. One grows at a constant 8% a year, the other by a constant €51.81 a year.

bloecke.titel: Forty years on a linear axis
bloecke.unter: Illustrative calculation. The straight line lies above the curve for almost the entire distance, and both end at the same amount.

bloecke.titel: The same data on a logarithmic axis
bloecke.unter: Illustrative calculation with the same figures as above. Constant percentage growth appears as a straight line. The series with a constant increase in euros bends downwards because its growth rate falls.

bloecke.md:
Both charts contain the same figures. On the linear axis, the series with a fixed increase in euros appears superior for almost four decades, and the compound interest curve looks like a flat run-up for twenty years. On the logarithmic axis, this impression is reversed. The 8% series is a straight line there because its growth rate is constant. The growth rate of the other series falls from 51.8% in the first year to 2.4% in the fortieth, which is why this series bends downwards.

This gives a reading rule for the logarithmic axis. A straight line means a constant growth rate, a line curving upwards means accelerating growth and a line curving downwards means slowing growth. Historical bubbles can therefore be recognised by the fact that the slope becomes steeper even on a logarithmic axis. On a linear chart, by contrast, every series that grows over the long term looks like a bubble at the right-hand edge.

- Most charting programs and almost all news graphics use a linear axis as the default. For periods of more than ten years, that is the wrong choice.
- A truncated y-axis magnifies movements. If the axis starts at 98 and ends at 102, a movement of 4% looks like a crash. You should therefore look at the axis labels first and only then at the curve.
- Unadjusted series contain jumps caused by share splits and distributions that are not genuine price movements. The DAX is usually shown as a total return index including dividends. However, it also exists as a price return index without dividends, and over decades the two curves diverge widely.

bloecke.titel: Illusion of control and hindsight bias
bloecke.md:
Behavioural research associates charts with the illusion of control. This refers to the tendency to experience random outcomes as controllable, and tools reinforce this impression. Langer demonstrated the effect in 1975 with lottery tickets. In 2003, Fenton-O'Creevy and colleagues studied traders at London investment banks. The individuals most prone to the illusion of control were rated lower in analysis and risk management, contributed less to profits and earned less.

In addition, there is hindsight bias. On a historical chart, every turning point looks obvious after the fact. A meaningful test is to cover the right-hand side of the chart and record a decision in writing candle by candle. Most patterns disappear in the process.

1. Clarify the axis type (linear or logarithmic); for more than ten years, use a logarithmic display.
2. Read off the axis range, that is, the start and end of the y-axis.
3. Match the timeframe to the time horizon of the question to be answered.
4. Choose the chart type. If the high and low are needed, a line chart is unsuitable.
5. Establish the trading venue and currency of price and volume.
6. Check the adjustment, that is, the type of series (price or total return series) and whether splits are taken into account.
A chart is based on a chosen condensation of the data and is not a fact. Chart type, timeframe and axis type determine which movement looks large, even before the first pattern is interpreted.

mitnehmen: Candlestick and bar charts contain the same four numbers per interval and differ only in how they display them.
The line chart shows neither the high nor the low, although stops, breakouts and volatility measures depend on these values.
The timeframe determines how often a trading decision arises and is thus the first cost decision of any strategy.
On a logarithmic axis, constant percentage growth appears as a straight line, which is why it is the only undistorted display for long periods.
A volume bar in a broker's chart reflects one trading venue and not the whole market, and in off-peak hours sometimes only a single order.

begriffe.text: Display that shows the open, high, low and close for each interval. The body lies between the open and the close, and the wicks extend to the high and the low. A candlestick chart contains the same information as a bar chart.
Thin line above and below the candle body. It marks the high and low of the interval, that is, prices that were reached but not held until the end of the interval.

Price range between the high of one interval and the low of the next (or vice versa) in which no trading took place. A price gap cannot be seen in a line chart, because it connects the closing prices without gaps.
Axis division in which equal vertical distances correspond to equal percentage changes. Constant percentage growth appears on it as a straight line, accelerating growth as an upward curve.

Pricing rule for exchange auctions. Orders are executed at the price at which the highest volume is achieved; in the event of a tie, the smaller surplus decides. On Xetra, the opening and closing prices are determined in this way.
